Adult narwhals exhibit a striking degree of sexual dimorphism in body size, a pattern commonly observed among odontocetes. Males ultimately attain a maximum wet body weight of 1,645,000 grams [Wwi = 1,645,000 grams], whereas females reach a considerably smaller ultimate wet weight of 904,000 grams [Wwi = 904,000 grams]. This pronounced size difference is thought to be linked to male-male competition for access to receptive females, with larger body size conferring an advantage during tusk displays and aggressive encounters. At birth, a narwhal calf weighs approximately 80,000 grams [Wwb = approximately 80,000 grams], a substantial neonatal mass that reflects the species' extended gestation and the advanced developmental state of the precocial newborn calf. The newborn calf is typically nursed by its mother in the dense pack ice of the Baffin Bay region, where the calf must quickly build a thick blubber layer to withstand the frigid Arctic waters.

The reproductive biology of the narwhal is characterized by an exceptionally slow pace of life, even by the standards of long-lived Arctic marine mammals. Females produce a single calf per litter [N_R_i = single calf per litter] and give birth once every two and a half years [F_R_i = half years], reflecting a low maximum reproductive rate that is consistent with the energetic demands of lactation in a cold, unproductive environment. The gestation period, during which the embryo develops within the uterus, has been documented to last 450 days [tg = 450 days] at the species' typical core body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This protracted gestation is among the longest recorded for any cetacean of comparable body size and is thought to allow for the extensive development of the large calf, which requires well-developed locomotor and sensory abilities to navigate the ice-choked nursery habitats.

At a core body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], narwhal development proceeds through several well-defined life history stages, each with characteristic timings that reflect the species' adaptation to a highly seasonal Arctic environment. Following birth, a nursing calf remains dependent on its mother's milk for an extended period, with weaning occurring at approximately 608 days after birth [tx = approximately 608 days after birth] at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This prolonged period of maternal investment allows the calf to acquire sufficient energy reserves and a thick blubber layer before it attains nutritional independence. The species' prolonged maturation is further evidenced by the age at which females first become reproductively viable; field data indicates that puberty in females is reached at about 2,372 days after birth [tp = about 2,372 days after birth], or roughly 6.5 years at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This delayed onset of reproductive capability underscores the high value placed on individual survival in a resource-limited environment.

Males follow a distinctly different developmental trajectory, with sexual maturation occurring considerably later than in females. Puberty in male narwhals is attained at approximately 3,285 days after birth [tp = approximately 3,285 days after birth], or roughly 9 years, at the same core body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This protracted period of maturation in males is a common pattern among polygynous or lekking mammals, where physical size and social rank are critical determinants of reproductive success. The delay allows males to continue growing for several additional years, thereby attaining the larger body dimensions characteristic of the species. This difference in maturation timing means that a cohort of male and female calves born in the same year will have substantially different reproductive trajectories, with females initiating breeding efforts several seasons before the males of their age class have even begun to compete for mating opportunities.

The maximum recorded longevity for narwhals provides further evidence of their slow life-history strategy. Females have been known to live for as long as 41,975 days [am = 41,975 days], a lifespan that is remarkable for a mammal of this body size at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This extreme longevity, maintained at a stable core body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], is believed to be an adaptation to the unpredictable and harsh conditions of the High Arctic, where a long reproductive career allows females to offset the costs of late maturation and a low annual fecundity. Males, by contrast, tend to have shorter lifespans, likely as a consequence of the energetic costs associated with intense male-male competition and the physical wear incurred by tusk use in social displays. This species thus exemplifies a classic bet-hedging strategy, where long-term survival and repeated breeding opportunities over many decades are prioritized over high short-term reproductive output.
